# Diagnosing a Stalled S15: From Stall to Fuel Smell

You are experiencing a classic sequence of events common to manual transmission owners, particularly those newer to the mechanics of an engine like the Nissan SR20DET found in an S15. The chain reaction began with an incomplete hill start, but the symptoms you are describingâshaking, power loss, high idle RPMs, and fuel odorâare distinct diagnostic markers pointing away from simple driver error and toward a specific mechanical failure: a flooded engine.

When you let go of the clutch too quickly, the torque converter (or in this case, the direct drive gears) engages before the engine has sufficient torque to overcome the load. This forces the engine speed to drop instantly. If the RPMs fall below the point where the fuel injectors can maintain a stable combustion cycle, the engine stalls. However, during that brief moment of engagement, the Engine Control Unit (ECU) likely detected a massive spike in Load and a sudden drop in RPM. To prevent the engine from stalling entirely, or perhaps due to a pre-existing idle air control issue, the ECU may have commanded a rich fuel mixtureâflooding the cylinders with gasoline rather than air.

The shaking you felt immediately after getting the car over the hill is the physical manifestation of unburned fuel in the combustion chamber. This condition is often called "wet compression." When the cylinder is filled with liquid fuel instead of an air-fuel mix, the spark plug cannot create a proper flame front. The engine struggles to complete its power stroke, resulting in a rough idle and significant vibration that transmits through the chassis and gear knob.

The sensation of lacking power and inability to reach higher RPMs confirms this diagnosis. A flooded engine creates excessive backpressure and reduces volumetric efficiency. The pistons are pushing against liquid fuel, which is nearly incompressible, rather than compressing a gaseous mixture that can be ignited efficiently. Consequently, the torque curve flattens out immediately.

The most critical symptom, however, is the smell of raw fuel coming from the exhaust. This indicates that the air-fuel ratio has deviated significantly into the rich side (Lambda > 1). The catalytic converter inside the exhaust system is now being starved of oxygen because it is trying to convert excess unburned hydrocarbons and carbon monoxide, but it cannot do so efficiently when the mixture is this lean. In fact, a flooded engine can temporarily overheat the catalytic converter or cause it to fail if left running for an extended period while flooded.

To resolve this situation without causing further damage, you must allow the unburned fuel to evaporate. Do not attempt to restart the engine immediately. The fuel system needs time to clear the excess liquid from the cylinders and intake manifold. Park the car in a well-ventilated area and let it sit for at least 15 to 30 minutes. During this time, you can lightly rev the engine if the car starts, but strictly limit the duration to no more than 10 seconds at a time to avoid drowning the catalytic converter further.

If the shaking persists after the fuel has evaporated, the issue may have shifted to spark plug fouling. Liquid fuel can coat the electrodes of your ignition plugs, preventing them from firing correctly even once the mixture is back to normal ratios. In this scenario, removing and inspecting the spark plugs is a necessary step. You will likely find black, wet deposits on the insulators. Cleaning or replacing these plugs will restore proper ignition timing and eliminate the shaking.

While this specific incident was caused by driver input on an S15, it serves as a reminder that engine management systems have limits. Even with modern ECU logic, rapid transitions from stall to load can overwhelm the fuel trims temporarily. If you find yourself struggling with hill starts consistently, consider installing an aftermarket idle air control valve or upgrading your clutch pedal feel to ensure smoother engagement points. The goal is always to keep the RPMs in a safe operating window before fully engaging the transmission.

If the fuel smell remains strong after several days of sitting, or if the check engine light illuminates with codes related to the oxygen sensor (P0420) or misfires (P0300 series), you may need to visit a mechanic to inspect the catalytic converter for thermal damage caused by the rich mixture event. Addressing these symptoms promptly prevents long-term corrosion in the exhaust system and ensures your SR20DET continues to deliver the performance it was designed for.
